Series::topk¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::topk(std::int64_t k) const -> Series
Series::topk(std::int64_t k, std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::topk(std::int64_t k, std::int64_t dim, bool largest) const -> Series
Series::topk(std::int64_t k, std::int64_t dim, bool largest, bool sorted) const -> Series

What It Does¶

topk() selects a partial ordering. It retains exactly k values from each lane rather than fully sorting every value. The selected axis remains in the result, but its size becomes k.

The default means “the largest k values on the final axis, in descending order.” largest=false selects the smallest side instead. sorted=false keeps the correct membership but removes the promise that selected values will be presented in rank order. Use topk_pair() when local source indices must accompany the selected values.

Parameters¶

k (std::int64_t): number of values to retain from each lane. It must lie between 0 and size(dim), inclusive.

dim (std::int64_t): selected axis; negative values count from the end.

largest (bool): choose the largest (true) or smallest (false) side of the order.

sorted (bool): request rank ordering of the selected values. It changes presentation guarantees, not which values are selected.

Returns¶

topk() returns selected values.

Gradient¶

topk() passes the selected values through unchanged, so its value channel is differentiable: the backward routes each output’s gradient to the input position that value came from, and every position outside the selected set receives 0. The selection boundary itself is discrete — which positions make the cut is held fixed during the backward pass, so no gradient flows through a rank exchange or a tie at the cutoff.

Examples¶

Example 1. The default retains the three largest values.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({3.0, 1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 5.0});
std::cout << scores.topk(3);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[5, 4, 3]

Example 2. largest=false takes the low end instead.

std::cout << scores.topk(3, 0, false, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1, 3]

Example 3. The selected axis changes length to k; every other axis stays.

auto table = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 1.0, 3.0}, {2.0, 5.0, 1.0}});
std::cout << table.topk(1, 0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[1,3], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=false)
data=[[4, 5, 3]]

Example 4. sorted=false does not weaken membership, only its display order.

std::cout << scores.topk(3, 0, true, false);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[5, 4, 3]

This run happens to be ordered. The sorted=false contract permits another valid ordering of the same three winners, so presentation code must not rely on this appearance.

Example 5. k=0 is valid and keeps an empty selected axis.

std::cout << scores.topk(0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[0], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=0, contiguous=true)
[]

Example 6. Asking for more winners than a lane contains fails.

try { std::cout << scores.topk(6); }
catch (const std::exception& error) { std::cout << error.what(); }

Output¶

topk: k must be <= size(dim)

Example 7. The value channel is differentiable; unselected positions get 0.

auto x = pluss::make_series({3.0, 1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 5.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto weights = pluss::make_series({100.0, 10.0, 1.0});
(x.topk(3, 0, true, true) * weights).sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 0.0000, 10.0000, 0.0000, 100.0000]

The three winners [5, 4, 3] came from positions [4, 2, 0], so they collect weights 100, 10, 1; the two unselected 1s at positions 1 and 3 get nothing.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • topk() is not a full sort; only the selected subset is guaranteed to be present.

  • sorted=false does not mean random and does not imply stable ordering.

  • Ties at the cutoff have no stable winner contract.

  • The value channel is differentiable; the selection boundary is not.

  • Complex-valued inputs are rejected.

Summary¶

Use topk() when only a small winning subset matters. Use sort() when every value must be ordered, and keep topk_pair() results when later code needs to recover the winning source positions.
